titles.angle: the channel's 'REAL' series — the question itself
titles.title: What Was The REAL Turning Point of WW1?
titles.hook: On 29 September 1918, Germany's two top generals told the Kaiser the front might not hold for two hours. Six months earlier they had been 56 km from Paris.
titles.why: The proven 'What was the REAL…' pattern; the thumbnail adds the twist the title holds back: the war was lost in 1917, not 1918.

titles.angle: one decision — the castle at Pless
titles.title: Did Germany REALLY Lose WW1 in a Castle in 1917?
titles.hook: On 9 January 1917, in a castle in Silesia, the Kaiser approved a plan to starve Britain in six months. Britain didn't starve. America came.
titles.why: A specific, surprising answer framed as a question; the six-month promise and the hourglass make the stakes readable at a glance.

titles.angle: myth vs truth — the stab in the back
titles.title: Was Germany's Army REALLY Stabbed in the Back in 1918?
titles.hook: Within months of the armistice, German officers said their army had never been beaten. So who asked for the armistice first?
titles.why: Myth-busting angle with a famous phrase; the timetable question ('who asked first?') is the provocation.

description:
What Was The REAL Turning Point of WW1?

On 29 September 1918, Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg and General Erich Ludendorff told Kaiser Wilhelm II that they could no longer guarantee the Western Front. Not for weeks. Not for days. For two hours. Six months earlier the same army had been about 56 kilometres from Paris.
So — when did Germany actually lose the First World War?

In this animated documentary a stationmaster of history keeps one hourglass for the whole war: every big German plan came with a deadline, and we stamp each candidate moment TURNED or NOT YET — looking at it from both sides of the wire.

Eight moments: the First Battle of the Marne and the end of the Schlieffen-Moltke plan, Joffre, Gallieni and Kluck's turn east of Paris; the British distant blockade, the Northern Patrol and the Turnip Winter; Falkenhayn's battle of attrition at Verdun, the Brusilov offensive and the first day of the Somme; Jutland, Scheer and Jellicoe; Holtzendorff's six-month promise, the decision at Pless for unrestricted submarine warfare, the Lusitania, the Zimmermann Telegram and America's declaration of war; the Russian Revolution and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk; Ludendorff's spring offensives, the stormtroopers and the Second Battle of the Marne under Foch; and Monash's attack at Amiens, the black day of the German Army. Then the armistice at Compiègne and the stab-in-the-back myth.

Our verdict: the Marne decided Germany could not win fast — Pless decided it could not win slowly.

In memory of the nine to eleven million soldiers, and the millions of civilians, who died in the First World War.

Sources include Wikipedia's articles on the First Battle of the Marne, the Blockade of Germany, the Turnip Winter, Verdun, the Somme, the Brusilov offensive, Jutland, unrestricted submarine warfare, Henning von Holtzendorff, the Zimmermann Telegram, the American entry into World War I, the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the German spring offensive, the Second Battle of the Marne, the Battle of Amiens, the Armistice of 11 November 1918 and the stab-in-the-back myth, and the BYU World War I Document Archive (Wilson's War Message). Casualty and blockade figures are estimates and are debated. The line attributed to Moltke in 1914 is unproven.
All scenes are animated illustrations, not archival footage.
